meta.title: Items and levels
meta.description: What an item is, how the level scale gives it its color and its rank, and what decides the order inside a shift.

basics.intro: An item is a plain object. Four fields are required — an id, a start, a level and a title — and everything else refines how the card reads. Items are placed into shifts by their start: one that falls outside every rendered shift is not shown, and one with an invalid start is dropped and reported once in development.

levels.intro: A level is a rank on a scale you define: what it is called, how strong it is, what color it carries and whether items of that rank pin when they scroll past. The package ships classicLevels, a nine-rank scale, but a scale of four ranks with your own keys is just as valid — and the keys flow into the item type, so a typo is a type error rather than a silent miss.
points: rank defaults to the position in the array, so a well-ordered array needs no ranks at all.
color and onColor default to the tokens --rs-level-{key} and --rs-level-{key}-on, which is how a theme can recolor a scale without touching the data.
variant picks the card treatment: 'alert' for the strongest rank, 'muted' for what is finished.
pinOnPass makes every item of that rank pin — see Pinning.
A label comes from localization.levels[key], so the scale is translated with the rest of the component.

order.intro: Inside a shift, items follow compareItems. The default is placement order: start, then level rank, then id. Replacing it changes the list, the timeline’s placement sequence and the pinned strip together, so the three never disagree about which item comes first.

points: A card’s accessible name carries its title, its level and its time, so the color of the rail is never the only thing that says how serious an item is.
Level and tag pills are text, not icons, and they are part of the card’s name.
A level’s color is only a reinforcement: the same information is in the label next to it.
The parts levelPill, tagPill and cardRail are replaceable through slots.
Colors live in the tokens --rs-level-* — see CSS variables.
tags defines the tags an item may carry, each with its own label and colors.
An item belongs to exactly one shift, the one its start falls in. An item that spans two shifts is drawn in the first and does not repeat in the second.
Duplicate ids are not merged: the first occurrence wins and the rest are dropped, with a warning in development.
The scale is flat — there is no grouping of levels into families, and no per-shift scale.
